basic_identification.name: Digital art conservation
basic_identification.originator: Variable Media Network (Jon Ippolito, Alain Depocas, 2000s). Rhizome (Mark Tribe, 1996; preservation director Dragan Espenschied). Tate (Patricia Falcao, time-based media conservation). Guggenheim (conservation department). LIMA Amsterdam. EMBARK network (EU COST Action, Joanna Phillips, 2024). Software Preservation Network. Key researchers: Pip Laurenson, Annet Dekker, Joanna Phillips.
basic_identification.year: 1999 (Rhizome ArtBase); 2003 (Variable Media approach formalized); 2024 (EMBARK pan-European network launched)
basic_identification.geography: North America and Europe primarily. Key institutions: Rhizome (New York), Tate (London), Guggenheim (New York), ZKM (Karlsruhe), LIMA (Amsterdam), RED Conservation Center (Dusseldorf). EMBARK brings together 25+ European countries. Significant gap in Asia, Africa, Latin America.

core_ideas.core_claim: Born-digital and time-based media artworks require fundamentally different conservation approaches than traditional art. The medium is inherently unstable: software becomes obsolete, hardware degrades, platforms disappear, file formats become unreadable. Conservation must preserve behavior and experience, not just material, through strategies including emulation, migration, documentation, and reinterpretation.
core_ideas.medium_specificity: This is the definitionally medium-specific field. The entire discipline exists because digital art's medium (software, hardware, networks) has a different relationship to time and permanence than traditional media. Unlike oil paint that slowly degrades, software can become instantly inaccessible when dependencies change. The conservation challenge is unique to digital: preserving something that never had material permanence.
core_ideas.relation_to_attention_economy: Resistant to attention economy. Conservation operates on deep-historical timescales incompatible with engagement metrics. The work is slow, technical, and largely invisible. There is a structural tension: the attention economy produces ephemeral digital culture at massive scale, while conservation resources are scarce and can only address a tiny fraction. The attention economy actively undermines conservation by normalizing impermanence.
core_ideas.relation_to_intention: Strongly intention-native. Conservation addresses the declared structural need to preserve cultural heritage. It is infrastructure work that serves the field's long-term knowledge requirements. No attention-capture motivation. The challenge is that intention-aligned work is chronically underfunded because it does not generate attention-economy returns.

market_economics.revenue_model: Primarily grant-funded and institutional. Rhizome: nonprofit, NEH grants, foundation support (Teiger Foundation), some fee-for-service preservation services. Tate/Guggenheim: museum budgets. EMBARK: EU COST Action grant (~600K EUR). LIMA: institutional collaboration fees. No market-based revenue model exists for digital art conservation. This is a public goods problem.
market_economics.market_position: Infrastructure, entirely upstream of markets. Conservation enables the long-term value of digital art but generates no direct market revenue.
market_economics.price_range: N/A. Conservation is a cost center, not a revenue generator. Individual preservation projects can cost thousands to hundreds of thousands of dollars depending on complexity.
market_economics.volume_trend_2024_2026: Growing need, insufficient capacity. The volume of born-digital art requiring conservation grows exponentially while conservation resources grow linearly at best. EMBARK's launch in 2024 represents growing institutional recognition. However, the gap between conservation need and conservation capacity continues to widen. [uncertain]
market_economics.collector_demographics: N/A directly. Conservation serves museums, archives, estates, and occasionally private collectors. The primary 'customers' are institutions with fiduciary responsibility to preserve collections.
market_economics.sustainability: Structurally unsustainable under current models. Grant funding is project-based, not ongoing. Museum budgets for digital conservation are typically insufficient. The expertise is scarce and scattered. The EMBARK network acknowledges that European institutions lack critical access to specialized research, expertise, and infrastructure. A sustainable model requires either endowed funding, shared infrastructure that distributes costs, or integration into standard institutional practice.

practice_aesthetics.toolchain: Archivematica (digital preservation system), BitCurator (born-digital curation), Conifer/Webrecorder (web archiving, note: Conifer discontinuing June 2026), Emulation-as-a-Service (EaaS) infrastructure, Media Info, QC Tools, PRONOM (file format registry), Variable Media Questionnaire, Media Art Notation System (MANS). Wikibase for collection metadata (Rhizome ArtBase). Software preservation tools from Software Preservation Network.
practice_aesthetics.relation_to_AI: Emerging. AI could assist with automated format identification, degradation detection, metadata extraction, and documentation. However, AI-based preservation tools are not yet mature. The conservation field is cautious about AI given concerns about interpretive fidelity: can an AI-migrated artwork preserve the artist's intent? AI-generated art creates new conservation challenges (how to preserve works dependent on specific model versions).
practice_aesthetics.liveness: The conservation object is often live, interactive, or performative: net art, interactive installations, software-based art, game art. The challenge of conserving 'liveness' is central: how do you preserve an interactive experience, not just a static artifact? Emulation attempts to preserve liveness by recreating the original execution environment.
practice_aesthetics.aesthetic_vocabulary: Technical-institutional: emulation, migration, reinterpretation, documentation, variable media, time-based media, significant properties, behavioral preservation, bit-level preservation, format migration, software dependency, hardware obsolescence, artist interview, installation specification. The vocabulary is adequate for technical conservation but less developed for the experiential and interpretive dimensions of what is being preserved.
practice_aesthetics.tendency_axis_position: Strongly open (most tools are open-source, knowledge is shared). Strongly commons (conservation knowledge is public good). Strongly infrastructure (definition of infrastructure). Mixed individual/collective: conservation of individual artworks through collective institutional effort.

infrastructure_governance.openness: Predominantly open. Rhizome's tools are open-source. Archivematica, BitCurator, and related tools are open. The Variable Media Questionnaire is a free web service. Research and methodologies are published openly. However, institutional conservation practices are often siloed and not systematically shared. The EMBARK network aims to address this fragmentation.
infrastructure_governance.governance_model: Institutional governance within individual organizations (museum boards, nonprofit boards). No centralized governance for the field. EMBARK provides the first pan-European coordination structure. The Digital Preservation Coalition offers industry coordination. Professional standards from AIC (American Institute for Conservation) and IIC (International Institute for Conservation). The field operates through professional consensus rather than formal governance.
infrastructure_governance.data_sovereignty: Complex. Artworks in institutional collections are typically controlled by the institution. Artist estates retain varying degrees of control. Conservation documentation is often institution-specific and not portable. The Variable Media Questionnaire and MANS attempt to create shared documentation standards. Rhizome's use of Wikibase enables linked data and SPARQL queries, moving toward more open data sovereignty.
infrastructure_governance.interoperability: Improving but insufficient. No universal conservation data standard. CIDOC Conceptual Reference Model (CIDOC-CRM) provides an ontological framework for cultural heritage but is complex to implement. Dublin Core and PREMIS provide metadata standards. Rhizome's Wikibase implementation enables SPARQL-queryable data. Most institutional conservation data remains in siloed, incompatible systems.
infrastructure_governance.preservation_strategy: This IS the preservation strategy for the field. Key approaches: (1) Emulation: recreating original execution environments via virtual machines (Guggenheim's Seeing Double, 2004; EaaS infrastructure). (2) Migration: converting works to current technologies (Flash to HTML5/JavaScript). (3) Documentation: artist interviews, installation specifications, behavioral descriptions. (4) Reinterpretation: allowing works to evolve with technology while maintaining artistic intent. Best practice combines multiple strategies.
infrastructure_governance.consent_architecture: Artist consent is central to conservation ethics. The Variable Media approach requires artist input on acceptable preservation strategies. Artist interviews document intentions and acceptable parameters for future conservation decisions. However, consent becomes impossible after an artist's death, creating a reliance on documented instructions. No machine-readable consent standard exists for conservation decisions.

field_position.relation_to_traditional_art_world: Embedded within traditional institutions but marginalized within them. Digital conservation departments exist at major museums (Tate, Guggenheim, Whitney, SFMOMA) but are typically understaffed and underfunded compared to traditional conservation. The conceptual frameworks draw from traditional conservation ethics (minimal intervention, reversibility, documentation) while acknowledging that digital media requires fundamentally different approaches.
field_position.what_it_enables: Long-term access to born-digital cultural heritage. Continued exhibition and scholarship of works whose original platforms no longer exist. Recovery of works thought lost to technological obsolescence. Institutional collecting of digital art (without conservation capacity, institutions cannot responsibly collect). Historical understanding of digital art's evolution.
field_position.what_it_lacks: Adequate funding and staffing. Standardized documentation formats. Shared infrastructure that reduces per-institution costs. Training programs adequate to meet demand (expertise is scarce). Tools for conserving AI-generated and AI-dependent art. Solutions for works dependent on proprietary services or live data feeds. Automated monitoring of collection health. Integration with blockchain provenance systems. Conservation approaches for works existing on decentralized infrastructure.
field_position.who_is_excluded: Artists outside major institutional collections (most digital art exists outside museums). Artists in regions without digital conservation infrastructure (most of the world). Artists whose work exists on platforms that may disappear without archival. Communities whose digital cultural practices fall outside Western art-historical frameworks. Independent collectors without access to conservation expertise. Future generations if current preservation efforts prove inadequate.
field_position.frontier_signal: Established as a discipline, frontier in implementation. The theoretical frameworks are mature (Variable Media, 20+ years). The frontier challenges are: scaling conservation to match the volume of born-digital art, addressing AI-art preservation, preserving blockchain-native art, building sustainable shared infrastructure, and extending beyond Western institutions.

attention_intention.discovery_mechanism: Academic publications, professional conferences (ICOM, AIC), institutional programs, word of mouth in conservation community. The EMBARK network provides a new coordination mechanism. Rhizome's editorial program brings some public visibility. Not discovered through social media algorithms.
attention_intention.attention_dependency: Very low. Conservation work continues regardless of public attention. The field's funding crisis is partly due to this low attention profile: preservation is invisible when it works and only noticed when it fails. Would be completely unaffected by social media disappearance.
attention_intention.intention_alignment: Maximally intention-aligned. Conservation is pure infrastructure work serving the long-term structural needs of the field. It generates no engagement metrics, no speculative returns, and no attention-economy value. This makes it simultaneously the most intention-aligned and most underfunded area of the digital art field.
attention_intention.commons_contribution: Strong. Open-source tools, published methodologies, shared documentation standards, community of practice. The EMBARK network is explicitly designed to make conservation knowledge a European commons. Rhizome's Wikibase ArtBase with SPARQL endpoint is exemplary commons infrastructure. However, individual institutional conservation data remains insufficiently shared.

provenance_temporality.provenance_type: Both ownership and meaning, partially. Conservation records track not just who owns a work but its exhibition history, condition changes, conservation interventions, and artist instructions. This approaches provenance of meaning. However, the focus is on the work's material/technical history rather than its interpretive or cultural reception history.
provenance_temporality.temporal_logic: Deep-historical and archival. Conservation operates on decades-to-centuries timescales. It is the only area of the digital art field that seriously engages with long-term temporality. The Variable Media approach explicitly addresses the question of what a work should be in the future, introducing an anticipatory dimension.
provenance_temporality.absence_handling: Conservation is acutely aware of absence: works already lost to technological obsolescence, documentation gaps, missing artist intentions, formats no longer readable. The field represents absence (noting what is unknown or unrecoverable) more rigorously than any other area of the digital art ecosystem. However, it primarily addresses absence at the individual work level rather than mapping systemic field-level absences.

coherence.coherence_vs_consensus: Coherence. The field accommodates multiple valid conservation approaches (emulation, migration, reinterpretation) without requiring consensus on which is best. The Variable Media approach explicitly allows different strategies for different works and contexts. Disagreements about best practice exist but within a coherent ethical framework.
coherence.contestability: Moderate. Conservation decisions can be contested by artists, curators, scholars, and future conservators. Artist interviews create a record of intent that can be referenced. However, once conservation actions are taken (especially migration), reversibility is limited. The power to make conservation decisions rests with institutions, which may not always reflect artist wishes or community values.
coherence.forkability: Conceptually yes (methodologies are open), practically limited. Conservation practices can be adopted by any institution, but the expertise, infrastructure, and relationships required create high barriers. You cannot simply fork Rhizome's preservation program without its 25 years of accumulated knowledge, relationships, and infrastructure.

adai_comparison.what_adai_should_adopt: The Variable Media approach to documenting not just what a work is but what it should remain: capturing behavior, experience, and intent alongside technical specifications. The deep-historical temporal logic that plans for decades, not quarters. The rigorous approach to documenting absence and uncertainty. Rhizome's use of Wikibase and linked data for collection metadata. The ethical framework that prioritizes artist intent and cultural heritage over market value.
adai_comparison.what_adai_should_refuse: The institutional gatekeeping that limits conservation to works already in museum collections. The siloed data practices that prevent cross-institutional knowledge sharing. The Western-centric institutional framework that excludes most of the world's digital cultural heritage. The narrow focus on individual artworks at the expense of preserving artistic practices, communities, and contexts.
adai_comparison.structural_tension: Digital art conservation preserves what exists but struggles to document what is missing. A(DAI) maps the field including its gaps, absences, and structural blind spots. Conservation focuses on the individual work; A(DAI) focuses on the field as a system. The productive tension is that A(DAI) can identify what needs preserving before it is lost, while conservation provides the methods to actually preserve it. Together they could create a system that anticipates preservation needs rather than responding to crises.

regulatory_legal.regulatory_exposure: Moderate. Copyright law affects conservation: creating copies for preservation may require legal exemptions. DMCA Section 108 provides limited exemptions for libraries and archives. The EU Digital Single Market Directive includes preservation exceptions. Moral rights (droit moral) affect how works can be altered during conservation. GDPR intersects when conservation records contain personal data. No regulation specifically addresses digital art conservation.
regulatory_legal.ip_model: Conservation operates within copyright law's limitations. Preservation copies are typically justified under library/archive exemptions. Emulation may require copying proprietary software, raising IP questions. Artist agreements increasingly include conservation permissions. Open-source conservation tools avoid IP encumbrances. The IP model is pragmatic rather than principled.
regulatory_legal.opt_in_vs_opt_out: Institutional: works in collections are conserved as part of the institution's mandate. Artist consent is sought when possible but not legally required in most jurisdictions once a work is in a collection. The artist's moral right to object to damaging treatment provides some protection. No formal opt-in/opt-out mechanism for conservation approaches.

ecosystem.platform_dependency: Depends on: open-source tool ecosystems (Archivematica, BitCurator), web standards (for web-based art), emulation infrastructure (EaaS), institutional IT infrastructure, and the continued existence of conservation expertise. Rhizome's discontinuation of Conifer (June 2026) illustrates how even specialized preservation tools can be lost. No single point of failure but many fragile dependencies.
ecosystem.network_effects: Positive network effects through shared knowledge and tools: more institutions doing conservation creates more shared expertise, better tools, and more sustainable infrastructure. The EMBARK network is explicitly designed to create these network effects across Europe. However, the field's small size limits network effects compared to commercial platforms.
ecosystem.post_crash_trajectory: Independent of NFT crash. The conservation crisis predates and will outlast market cycles. If anything, the post-crash period has been positive: institutions can focus on long-term preservation rather than being distracted by speculative markets. Growing institutional recognition (EMBARK launch 2024, Harvard DAP 2024) suggests increased investment. However, the gap between need and capacity continues to widen.
